group.passage:
Have you ever heard people talk about a past event, only to learn that their memories differ from the actual facts? This phenomenon is known as the Mandela Effect. The term was coined by Fiona Broome, who noticed that she and others remembered Nelson Mandela dying in prison during the 1980s, even though he actually passed away in 2013 after serving as South Africa’s president. These shared false memories have long fascinated both scientists and the general public.
Psychologists believe the Mandela Effect stems from the way human memory works. Instead of storing perfect copies of events, our brains reconstruct memories using fragments of information and prior expectations. Psychologists often explain this using two main ideas: “source monitoring error” and “schema theory.” A source monitoring error occurs when people misremember where a memory originated. For example, they might think they saw something on the news when they actually heard about it in a conversation. Schema theory, on the other hand, suggests that the brain fills gaps with familiar patterns, sometimes producing false memories that feel entirely real.
One well-known example of the Mandela Effect comes from a children’s book series called The Berenstain Bears. Many people recall the name spelled as “Berenstein,” with “-stein” being a more common spelling in English. However, the correct spelling has always been “Berenstain.” Our brain might unconsciously change the memory to match more familiar patterns. This widespread misremembering, shared by thousands of readers, shows how false memories can influence groups, not just individuals.
Some people propose more imaginative theories to explain the Mandela Effect. One involves parallel universes—suggesting there may be other versions of our world where events unfolded differently. According to this theory, those who experience the Mandela Effect may have memories from another universe. While not supported by scientific evidence, this idea is often explored in fiction and highlights how mysterious memory—and the universe—can be.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?

options.A: The Mandela Effect proves that parallel universes may be real.
options.B: Memory errors are often influenced by what people hear from others.
options.C: False memories are often caused by repeated exposure to certain information.
options.D: Shared false memories suggest that memory is reconstructive rather than accurate.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what do source monitoring error and schema theory have in common?

options.A: Both explain why people forget specific names or dates.
options.B: Both show that memory mistakes happen only to individuals.
options.C: Both involve the brain creating or altering memory content.
options.D: Both suggest that false memories are influenced by mass media.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention the theory of parallel universes in the final paragraph?

options.A: To propose it as a scientific explanation of memory errors.
options.B: To introduce a popular but unproven idea about the Mandela Effect.
options.C: To demonstrate that memory theories are often based on personal beliefs.
options.D: To suggest that psychological theories alone can fully explain the Mandela Effect.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of the Mandela Effect?

options.A: A high school student consistently misspells the word “separate” as “saperate”.
options.B: Consumers recall the famous candy brand name “Kit Kat” with a hyphen as “Kit-Kat”.
options.C: Movie fans recall Snow White’s queen saying “Mirror, mirror on the wall” instead of “Magic mirror on the wall”.
options.D: Some players believe the Monopoly man wears a small eyepiece, though he never has.
